# Warm up

## Participate  {.smaller}

Which of the following is **true** about the code below?

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| message: false
ggplot(flights, _[blank]_(x = dep_time, y = dep_delay)) +
  geom_point()
```

a. `flights` is the name of the variable being plotted on the x-axis
b. The function that goes in the [blank] is `map`
c. The data are being visualized with a scatterplot
d. Some points on the plot will be colored differently than others

# From last time

## Start with the question {.smaller}

| Question | Variables | A useful first plot |
|---|---|---|
| What values are common? | One categorical | [Bar chart]{.fragment} |
| What is the distribution? | One numerical | [Histogram or boxplot]{.fragment} |
| Do groups differ? | Numerical + categorical | [Boxplot or histogram by group]{.fragment} |
| Are two categorical variables associated? | Two categorical | [Filled or dodged bar chart]{.fragment} |
| Are two numerical variables associated? | Two numerical | [Scatterplot]{.fragment} |

## Interesting Questions <-> many variables {.xsmall}

Bring the third, fourth, fifth, etc. variable to the plot using additional aesthetics such as `color`, `shape`, `size`, `linewidth`, etc. and/or with faceting (creating small multiple plots based on the levels of a variable):

```{r}
#| label: four-vars
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-asp: 0.5
#| fig-width: 9
library(tidyverse)
gss <- read_csv("data/gss-2024.csv")
gss |>
  filter(!is.na(happiness), !is.na(health)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = age, x = happiness, color = health, fill = health)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~marital_status, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Happiness, health, and age",
    y = "Age (years)",
    x = "Happiness",
    color = "Health",
    caption = "Source: 2024 General Social Survey (GSS), NORC"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  ggthemes::scale_colour_colourblind() +
  ggthemes::scale_fill_colourblind() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(10))
```

## Data frames and variables

-   Each row of a data frame is an **observation**

. . .

-   Each column of a data frame is a **variable**


## `gss` data frame {.smaller}

```{r}
gss
```

## `health` variable {.smaller}

```{r}
gss$health
```

## Participate {.smaller}

Why did the error occur?

```{r}
#| label: happiness-error
#| error: true
happiness
```

a. Name of the variable is misspelled
b. There is no such variable in the gss data frame
c. Must refer to variable in a data frame with `$`:   `gss$happiness`
d. Must refer to variable in a data frame with `|>`:   `gss |> happiness`
e. Must refer to variable in a data frame with `$`:   `happiness$gss`


## `function(argument)`

Functions are (most often) verbs, followed by what they will be applied to in parentheses, and separated by commas:

```{r}
#| eval: false
do_this(to_this)
do_that(to_this, to_that, with_those)
```


# Data transformation

## A grammar of data wrangling... {.smaller}

... based on the concepts of functions as verbs that manipulate data frames

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/04/dplyr-part-of-tidyverse.png)
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
- `select`: pick columns by name
- `filter`: pick rows matching criteria
- `mutate`: add new variables
- `summarize`: reduce variables to values
- `group_by`: for grouped operations
- `arrange`: reorder/sort rows
- `distinct`: filter for unique rows
- ... (many more)
:::

::: 

## Rules of **dplyr** functions

- First argument is always a data frame (we'll use the **pipe** `|>` instead)
- They don't modify the data frame in place
- (Instead, they return a new data frame)

## Example {.smaller}

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|2|3"
gss |> # <1>
  filter(age > 45) |> # <2>
  select(age, employment_status, party_id, happiness) # <3>
```

1.  Start with the `gss` data frame
2.  Filter for respondents older than 45
3.  Select the columns `age`, `employment_status`, `party_id`, and `happiness`

## Participate {.smaller}

In data transformation with the pipe operator `|>`, what does the operator do?

a) It ends a pipeline and prints the result.
b) It joins two data frames together.
c) It passes the output from the previous command into the first argument of the function in the next command.
d) It is equivalent to the "or" operator.

## The pipe `|>` {.smaller}

The pipe operator passes what comes before it into the function that comes after it as the first argument in that function.

::: columns

::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
sum(1, 2)
```

:::

::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
1 |>
  sum(2)
```

:::

:::

<br>

::: columns

::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
select(filter(gss, age > 50), health)
```

:::

::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
gss |>
  filter(age > 50) |>
  select(health)
```

:::

:::

## Code style tip {{< fa lightbulb >}} {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

In data **transformation** pipelines, always use a

-   space before `|>`
-   line break after `|>`
-   indent next line of code

:::

::: {.column .fragment}

In data **visualization** layers, always use a

-   space before `+`
-   line break after `+`
-   indent next line of code

:::

:::


## The pipe, in action

::: task
Write a single pipeline to find respondents who are living the dream: retired, in excellent health, very happy, and younger than 50 years old. 

Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have. Arrange the rows in increasing order of age.
:::

## The pipe - Step 1 {.small}

::: {.task .xsmall}
Write a single pipeline to find respondents who are living the dream: retired, in excellent health, very happy, and younger than 50 years old. Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have.
:::

Start with the `gss` data frame:

```{r}
gss
```

## The pipe - Step 2 {.small}

::: {.task .xsmall}
Find respondents who are living the dream: **retired**, in excellent health, very happy, and younger than 50 years old. Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have.
:::

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
gss |>
  filter(employment_status == "Retired")
```

## The pipe - Step 3 {.small}

::: {.task .xsmall}
Find respondents who are living the dream: retired, **in excellent health**, very happy, and younger than 50 years old. Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have.
:::

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
gss |>
  filter(
    employment_status == "Retired",
    health == "Excellent"
  )
```

## The pipe - Step 4 {.small}

::: {.task .xsmall}
Find respondents who are living the dream: retired, in excellent health, **very happy**, and younger than 50 years old. Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have.
:::

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "5"
gss |>
  filter(
    employment_status == "Retired",
    health == "Excellent",
    happiness == "Very happy"
  )
```

## The pipe - Step 5 {.small}

::: {.task .xsmall}
Find respondents who are living the dream: retired, in excellent health, very happy, and **younger than 50 years old**. Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have.
:::

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "6"
gss |>
  filter(
    employment_status == "Retired",
    health == "Excellent",
    happiness == "Very happy",
    age < 50
  )
```

## The pipe - Step 7 {.small}

::: {.task .xsmall}
Find respondents who are living the dream: retired, in excellent health, very happy, and younger than 50 years old. **Display their ages, employment statuses, health statuses, happiness levels, and the number of children they have.**
:::

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "8"
gss |>
  filter(
    employment_status == "Retired",
    health == "Excellent",
    happiness == "Very happy",
    age < 50
  ) |>
  select(age, employment_status, health, happiness, children)
```
